papers.title: Simulated Annealing with Topological Spatial Chunking for De Novo Protein Sequence Design
papers.abstract: The inverse protein folding problem, designing a discrete amino acid sequence that spontaneously folds into a predefined macroscopic structure, remains a phenomenally demanding combinatorial challenge central to synthetic drug discovery. While algorithms like SA offer a baseline approach for navigating dense biomolecular energy landscapes, applying SA heuristics to large sequences is inherently frustrated by exponentially large search spaces and deep local energy minima. This study proposes a scalable sequence design architecture, Topological Spatial Chunking Simulated Annealing, based on a localized, exact-solving heuristic embedded within a global simulated-annealing wrapper. To fundamentally circumvent exponential scaling walls, we deploy a dynamic solver that segments the global molecular target into shallow, k-variable algorithmic windows. Crucially, rather than partitioning natively by sequential 1D chronology, we introduce topological spatial chunking, which dynamically groups discrete variables based on Euclidean spatial proximity to preserve critical non-local thermodynamic correlations. The spatially localized sub-problems are solved deterministically via exact enumeration, while the global traversal is securely regulated by an exterior simulated annealing governor augmented by dynamic reheating and continuous elitism caching. We comprehensively benchmarked this classical architecture on the standard HP biophysical lattice against targeted 20-merA, 25-mer, 50-mer, and 64-mer geometries. Most notably, when evaluating the computationally exhaustive 50-mer and 64-mer topologies, the framework successfully bypassed widely accepted heuristic boundaries. By leveraging deterministic exact solving to vault classical energy traps, the system algorithmically resolved a novel, ultra-dense sequence-packing configuration for the 50-mer, defining a new theoretical global optimum.

papers.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
papers.abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

papers.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
papers.abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

papers.title: The Sharpness Disparity Principle in Transformers for Accelerating Language Model Pre-Training
papers.abstract: Transformers consist of diverse building blocks, such as embedding layers, normalization layers, self-attention mechanisms, and point-wise feedforward networks. Thus, understanding the differences and interactions among these blocks is important. In this paper, we uncover a clear Sharpness Disparity across these blocks, which emerges early in training and intriguingly persists throughout the training process. Motivated by this finding, we propose Blockwise Learning Rate (LR), a strategy that tailors the LR to each block's sharpness, accelerating large language model (LLM) pre-training. By integrating Blockwise LR into AdamW, we consistently achieve lower terminal loss and nearly $2\times$ speedup compared to vanilla AdamW. We demonstrate this acceleration across GPT-2 and LLaMA, with model sizes ranging from 0.12B to 2B and datasets of OpenWebText, MiniPile, and C4. Finally, we incorporate Blockwise LR into Adam-mini (Zhang et al., 2024), a recently proposed memory-efficient variant of Adam, achieving a combined $2\times$ speedup and $2\times$ memory saving. These results underscore the potential of exploiting the sharpness disparity to improve LLM training.

papers.title: Fast Catch-Up, Late Switching: Optimal Batch Size Scheduling via Functional Scaling Laws
papers.abstract: Batch size scheduling (BSS) plays a critical role in large-scale deep learning training, influencing both optimization dynamics and computational efficiency. Yet, its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that the functional scaling law (FSL) framework introduced in Li et al. (2025a) provides a principled lens for analyzing BSS. Specifically, we characterize the optimal BSS under a fixed data budget and show that its structure depends sharply on task difficulty. For easy tasks, optimal schedules keep increasing batch size throughout. In contrast, for hard tasks, the optimal schedule maintains small batch sizes for most of training and switches to large batches only in a late stage. To explain the emergence of late switching, we uncover a dynamical mechanism -- the fast catch-up effect -- which also manifests in large language model (LLM) pretraining. After switching from small to large batches, the loss rapidly aligns with the constant large-batch trajectory. Using FSL, we show that this effect stems from rapid forgetting of accumulated gradient noise, with the catch-up speed determined by task difficulty. Crucially, this effect implies that large batches can be safely deferred to late training without sacrificing performance, while substantially reducing data consumption. Finally, extensive LLM pretraining experiments -- covering both Dense and MoE architectures with up to 1.1B parameters and 1T tokens -- validate our theoretical predictions. Across all settings, late-switch schedules consistently outperform constant-batch and early-switch baselines.

papers.title: Mean-field Token Steering
papers.abstract: We consider stochastic token steering through a deep stack of transformer layers as a mean-field control problem for an interacting particle system on the unit sphere, where interactions arise from the attention mechanism. In the mean-field limit, the token population evolves via a controlled integro-partial differential equation where the feedback control acts as a corrective vector field guiding the population toward an aggregate configuration of tokens in the representation space. We deduce the minimum effort control to accomplish this task over a fixed time horizon interpreted as normalized layer depth. We show that the resulting controlled dynamics for the token population can be understood as a mean-field Schr\"odinger bridge adapted to the sphere geometry. Building on this, we propose a novel generalization of the dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute the consistent token evolution. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves exact steering of the token population.

papers.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

papers.title: Ensemble Modeling for Time Series Forecasting: an Adaptive Robust Optimization Approach
papers.abstract: Accurate time-series forecasting is critical for many problems involving temporal data. Ensemble modeling is a well-established technique that leverages multiple predictive models to improve accuracy and robustness, since a single predictor's performance can vary widely due to shifts in the underlying data distribution. This paper proposes a new methodology for building robust ensembles of time series forecasting models. Our approach uses Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) to construct a linear regression ensemble whose model weights adapt over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through synthetic experiments covering eight disturbance scenarios, from no drift to abrupt regime shifts, and real-world applications, including air pollution management, energy consumption forecasting, and tropical cyclone intensity forecasting. In the real-world applications, our adaptive ensembles outperform the best ensemble member in hindsight by 16-26% in root mean square error (RMSE) and 14-28% in conditional value at risk at the 15% level and improve over the other ensemble methods we compare on most metrics. In the synthetic experiments, they have lower mean RMSE than a rolling-ridge comparator in seven of the eight scenarios, significantly in four, while an abrupt regime shift that first appears after model selection remains a limitation.

papers.title: Data-Driven Exploration for a Class of Continuous-Time Indefinite Linear--Quadratic Reinforcement Learning Problems
papers.abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) for a class of continuous-time stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) control problems, where volatilities depend on both states and controls while states are scalar-valued and there are no running control rewards, the last feature also leading to the so-called indefinite LQ controls. We propose a model-free, data-driven exploration mechanism that adaptively adjusts entropy regularization by the critic and policy variance by the actor. Unlike the constant or deterministic exploration schedules employed in the existing literature, which require extensive tuning for implementations and ignore learning progress during iterations, our adaptive exploratory approach boosts learning efficiency with minimal tuning. Despite its flexibility, our method achieves a sublinear regret bound that matches the best-known model-free results for this class of LQ problems, which were previously derived only with fixed exploration schedules. Numerical experiments demonstrate that adaptive explorations accelerate convergence and improve regret performance compared to the non-adaptive model-free and model-based counterparts.

papers.title: Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Asset-Liability Management
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for Asset-Liability Management (ALM) by employing continuous-time Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a linear-quadratic (LQ) formulation that incorporates both interim and terminal objectives. We develop a model-free, policy gradient-based soft actor-critic algorithm tailored to ALM for dynamically synchronizing assets and liabilities. To ensure an effective balance between exploration and exploitation with minimal tuning, we introduce adaptive exploration for the actor and scheduled exploration for the critic. Our empirical study evaluates this approach against two enhanced traditional financial strategies, a model-based continuous-time RL method, and three state-of-the-art RL algorithms. Evaluated across 200 randomized market scenarios, our method achieves higher average rewards than all alternative strategies, with rapid initial gains and sustained superior performance. The outperformance stems not from complex neural networks or improved parameter estimation, but from directly learning the optimal ALM strategy without learning the environment.

papers.title: DualHash: Stochastic Primal-Dual Algorithms for W-Type Regularized Deep Hashing
papers.abstract: Deep hashing encodes high-dimensional image features into compact binary codes, enabling efficient similarity search in large-scale content-based image retrieval, a problem akin to semantic-preserving lossy compression under extreme bit-rate constraints. A fundamental challenge in deep hashing stems from the discrete nature of quantization in generating the codes. W-type regularizations, such as $z\mapsto\||z|-1\|_1$, are widely adopted and empirically effective at pushing network outputs toward binary values. However, existing methods often directly optimize these regularizations without convergence guarantees. While proximal gradient methods offer a promising solution, the coupling between W-type regularizers and neural network outputs results in composite forms that generally lack closed-form proximal solutions. In this paper, using Fenchel duality, we reformulate the nonconvex W-type regularization term through its convex conjugate, yielding a min-max problem with tractable proximal updates. We show that this min-max problem captures the stationarity of the original deep hashing objective up to the quantization error. Building on this problem, we present a stochastic primal-dual hashing algorithm, referred to as DualHash, with oracle complexity guarantees. We derive two algorithm instances: a momentum-based version with $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ oracle complexity and an improved $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ version using variance reduction, both for $\varepsilon$-KKT points of the min-max problem, which yield near-stationarity guarantees for the original objective. Experiments on three standard datasets demonstrate competitive retrieval accuracy and reduced quantization error, validating the practical value of DualHash for image retrieval problems. Our implementation of DualHash is available at https://github.com/RailLee/DualHash.

papers.title: Adaptive Reparametrized Time for Score-Based Diffusion Sampling
papers.abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where the learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard, but their fixed, ad hoc prescriptions can be suboptimal. We propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating sampling-clock speed as the control, so a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in diffusion time and a leading-order Euler error surrogate defines the allocation objective. To solve the resulting high-dimensional deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized Gaussian-policy formulation that turns schedule learning into continuous-time reinforcement learning. We prove ART-RL is equivalent to ART at optimality: the mean of the optimal Gaussian policy solves ART. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor-critic updates. Experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation show that ART-learned schedules, when plugged into existing samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improve sample quality over strong baselines at matched budgets. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalizability, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, data sets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

papers.title: The Shadow Price of Intelligence: Quality Degradation and Retry Feedback in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Large language model providers are compute constrained, and a common response to congestion is to degrade service: route queries to smaller models, cut reasoning budgets, or shorten context windows. A user who receives an unsatisfactory answer either retries, adding load while the system is busy, or abandons, possibly as churn. We model inference serving as a control problem in which service quality is the provider's decision. A two-regime fluid approximation with retries folded into the service rate gives closed-form trajectories and crossing times, so the dynamic program over quality tiers needs no simulation. We characterize a region in which a weaker tier uses less energy per task but more capacity per task, and show that in the fluid model reactive throttling to such a tier can keep the queue from draining. With heterogeneous customers the problem is a transportation problem with retry-inflated capacity coefficients; optimal routing follows a $c\mu$-type index, and the dual of the capacity constraint gives the marginal cost of one more query by class and time. We illustrate the method on five instances calibrated to public benchmark data.

papers.title: When Should a Human Take Back Control? Optimal Delegation under Turbulent AI Risk
papers.abstract: When should a human take control from an autonomous AI agent, how much checking is worthwhile, and when should autonomy resume? These decisions become harder when incidents cluster and recent errors signal elevated risk. Exploratory analyses of AgentLogs coding-agent traces and ODCV-Bench task runs show higher held-out log likelihood for Hawkes incident-history models than matched no-history baselines, with positive gains whose conditional $90\%$ intervals exclude zero. AgentLogs evaluates continuous-time incident timing and type; ODCV evaluates failure occurrence at discrete decisions. Motivated by this predictive evidence, we formulate a continuous-time delegation problem that jointly chooses productive action, verification effort, and switching rates between human-directed, AI-assisted operation and autonomous AI operation. The model assumes that verification weakens incident propagation and balances project benefits against operating, supervision, risk, and handoff costs. Our Hawkes-PPO method summarizes observed incidents with exponential memory filters and learns these decisions from rewards. In synthetic experiments, it achieves a higher evaluated objective than either fixed regime and PPO without history filters, and approaches an approximate full-information benchmark. Further experiments show how incident excitation and supervision costs shape delegation.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
papers.abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

papers.title: Strengthening Compact Vehicle Routing Formulations through Arc-Flow Aggregation and Refinement
papers.abstract: Arc-flow formulations can provide strong relaxations for mixed-integer program formulations of vehicle routing problems, but the associated networks may be prohibitively large. We study the setting in which multiple arc flow relaxations may be applied, and introduce a dual-guided aggregation and refinement framework that constructs substantially smaller arc-flow formulations while recovering the LP bound of the original networks. Dual information is used both to identify states that can be aggregated without weakening the bound and to guide node disaggregation. We show that the resulting procedure converges finitely to the arc-flow bound of the full arc-flow formulation. The framework retains the original decision variables, allowing cutting planes to be added directly in the original variable space. Moreover, it produces an explicit MILP formulation without relying on column generation or pricing to determine the arc-flow relaxation bound. We apply our approach to the vehicle routing problem with time windows for which we define two arc flow relaxations, as well as two families of cutting planes over the original variable space. Computational experiments show that strong bounds can be obtained using substantially aggregated networks. The resulting root bounds are competitive with those obtained by the branch-and-price solver RouteOpt, while retaining a formulation that can be solved directly by a general-purpose MILP solver.

papers.title: Odd faces as a parameter for maximum independent set in embedded graphs
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a maximum weight independent set in a graph embedded in a surface of bounded genus and with a bounded number of vertex-disjoint odd faces. In particular, we obtain an algorithm for graphs with an even-faced embedding in a torus and for planar graphs with a bounded number of odd faces, answering a question of Thomass\'e (2018) and a question of Choi, Gorsky, Kim, McFarland, and Wiederrecht (2025) respectively. We reduce the original problem to finding a minimum cost non-negative integer circulation with homology constraints in the dual of a certain double cover of the original graph.

papers.title: Log-Averaged Mirror Prox for Fast, Large-Scale Optimal Transport in Linear Space
papers.abstract: We propose Log-Averaged Mirror Prox (LAMP), a linear-space primal-dual method for large-scale optimal transport. LAMP implements primal mirror prox updates by tracking an averaged dual sequence, reducing storage complexity from $\mathcal{O}(nm)$ to $\mathcal{O}(n+m)$ while preserving dense, GPU-friendly reductions. Consequently, LAMP preserves the last-iterate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\|C\|_\infty nm\varepsilon^{-1})$ arithmetic complexity of conservatively parameterized primal-dual mirror prox. We further analyze LAMP as a direct optimal transport solver in a more performant parameter regime, providing a last-iterate sub-optimality certificate dependent on infeasibility and an explicit $\mathcal O(\|C\|_\infty\log (m)/t)$ term. Moreover, we give a computable sufficient condition for ergodic convergence. Numerical experiments with an optimized CUDA implementation show that LAMP outperforms first-order baselines in several high-accuracy (entropic) optimal transport problems. LAMP is further shown to scale up to problems with $n=m=2^{18}$ marginal supports, which were previously beyond the reach of primal-dual first-order methods.

papers.title: Constrained and Composite Sampling via Proximal Sampler
papers.abstract: We study two log-concave sampling problems: constrained sampling and composite sampling. First, we consider sampling from a distribution proportional to $e^{-f}$ on a convex set $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, where $f$ is convex. Using an epigraph lifting, we reduce this problem to uniform sampling up to a one-dimensional exponential tilt over a convex set in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. We then apply the proximal sampler to the lifted distribution. We develop an unbiased implementation of its restricted Gaussian oracle by using the cutting-plane method and rejection sampling, requiring only a separation oracle for $K$ and evaluation and subgradient oracles for $f$, without relying on projections or barrier functions. Second, we study composite sampling from $e^{-f-h}$, where $f$ and $h$ are closed and convex. This structure arises naturally in Bayesian inference, where $f$ represents data fidelity and $h$ encodes prior information. By applying an epigraph lifting to $h$, we reduce composite sampling to constrained sampling in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, allowing us to build on the approach developed in the first part. This leads to a double lifting formulation in $\mathbb R^{d+2}$, for which we implement the proximal sampler using different combinations of subgradient and proximal oracles for $f$ and $h$. We establish mixing time bounds in R\'enyi and $\chi^2$ divergences for both problems. Finally, we revisit the convergence analysis of the proximal sampler from a variational perspective. Starting from variational formulations of its two half-steps as optimization problems over probability measures, we use a dynamic formulation of entropy-regularized optimal transport to recast them as optimal control problems. This allows us to derive their governing PDEs directly through the lens of optimization, without first analyzing particle-level SDEs.

papers.title: Integer Programming Parametrized by Imbalanced Circuit Packing
papers.abstract: We study the standard form Integer Programming problem (IP) parametrized by the imbalanced circuit packing number. This number is $0$ if and only if $A$ can be transformed to a totally unimodular matrix by row operations, in which case (IP) is solvable in polynomial time. We show that if the constraint matrix represents a graphic matroid, (IP) is fixed-parameter tractable when parametrized by the imbalanced circuit packing number of the matrix. The proof combines an Erd\H{o}s-P\'osa property for edge-colored non-monochromatic cycles with a reduction to mixed-integer programming using few integer variables. In contrast, by a reduction from the parity potential problem, we show NP-completeness of feasibility of (IP) when the constraint matrix represents a cographic matroid, even if kernel of the constraint matrix is $2$-regular and imbalanced circuits pairwise intersect.

papers.title: Two-Sided Projection-Based Model Reduction of Parametric Generalized Algebraic Riccati Equations via Grassmann-Manifold Optimization
papers.abstract: Parametric generalized algebraic Riccati equations arise in many-query problems in optimal control, state estimation, and filtering, where repeated full-order solutions may become computationally prohibitive for large-scale systems. In this paper, within a projection-based model reduction framework, we propose a two-sided projection approach that constructs reduced bases by minimizing the aggregate relative two-sided projection error of Riccati solution snapshots. Under suitable dissipativity assumptions, the resulting Galerkin-projected PGARE admits a unique symmetric positive semidefinite stabilizing solution. For error assessment, we employ an existing residual-based a posteriori error estimator for the full-order Riccati residual. A projection-based error decomposition developed in this work provides the theoretical motivation for the proposed basis construction. To accommodate clustered solution manifolds, we extend the framework to localized model reduction by combining parameter-space proximity and solution-space correlation for clustering, with classifier-based online basis selection. Numerical experiments on parameterized heat-conduction problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed global and localized approaches in terms of approximation accuracy and computational efficiency.

papers.title: NeRI: Neural Residual Iteration for Elliptic Operator Equations and Variational Inequalities
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose a so-called {\it Neural Residual Iteration} (NeRI), a weak-form neural-network framework for solving a class of elliptic operator equations and variational inequalities, including nonlinear and nonsymmetric problems that may not admit a global energy functional. The key idea is to construct, at each iteration, a state-dependent linear functional whose derivative with respect to the trial function recovers the current weak residual. A single gradient step is then performed on the residual, yielding a residual-driven neural update without requiring a global energy functional or an additional test network. From a function-space perspective, NeRI can be interpreted as a neural-tangent-kernel-preconditioned realization of classical residual iterations, thereby bridging classical iterative solvers and neural-network optimization. We further extend NeRI to elliptic variational inequalities (VIs) through penalized and constraint-preserving formulations. For wide two-layer networks under gradient flow, we prove finite-time lazy-training estimates and derive an $H^1$-error decomposition relative to the exact weak solution. Numerical experiments on several elliptic problems demonstrate the effectiveness of NeRI, particularly for nonsymmetric and low-regularity problems.

papers.title: Martingale and signed diffusive optimal transport: geodesics and gradient flows
papers.abstract: In signed diffusive transport, a path of probability densities $\rho_t$ on the circle and a momentum $m_t$ satisfy $\partial_t\rho=\partial_{xx}m$, and the cost of the path is the action $\int_0^1\int m^2/(2\rho)\,dx\,dt$. The diffusivity $m/\rho$ is an unknown of this variational problem and can take either sign. On the real line, the constraint $m\ge0$ gives the martingale Benamou-Brenier problem of Huesmann and Trevisan. We study geodesics and minimizing movements, which discretize gradient flows. For signed geodesics, we prove the $\Gamma$-convergence of the time-discrete problems for all probability endpoints, and of the fully discrete Fourier-grid problems as the space and time meshes tend to zero independently, without a positive lower bound on the densities. For a modified Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme on the torus, we prove convergence along subsequences to a weak solution of a fourth-order equation, the Derrida-Lebowitz-Speer-Spohn equation for the entropy in dimension one, under the assumption that the densities of the scheme stay above a positive constant on every finite time interval. In dimension one, the normalized minimum values of a discretization with nonnegative momentum and of a discretization by martingale couplings with a fourth-moment cost converge to the same martingale transport cost, and we identify the limit of the minimizing movements with nonnegative momentum for potential energies with bounded second and third derivatives. We compute geodesics and modified JKO trajectories by Douglas-Rachford splitting and by an interior-point method, and bound the optimization errors of selected solutions by dual lower bounds evaluated in interval arithmetic. The computed geodesics approach zero density near the points where the diffusivity changes sign, and along computed trajectories of the modified JKO scheme the density minimum can fall below its initial value.

papers.title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
papers.abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.

papers.title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
papers.abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-\gamma)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/\delta))$ samples, where $S, A, \gamma, \delta$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/\delta))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/\delta))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

papers.title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging with Multi-Source Data
papers.abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model from distributed client data. The deployment risk is typically specified through two approximations: each unknown local distribution is replaced by its empirical distribution, and the unknown deployment mixture across clients is replaced by empirical or prescribed training weights. Existing robust methods usually address one approximation at a time through local distributional ambiguity sets or worst-case client mixtures. However, joint treatment of both approximations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct a global ambiguity set formed by admissible mixtures of client-wise Wasserstein ambiguity sets, yielding a distributionally robust optimization formulation. The construction allows client-dependent ambiguity radii, preserves client-wise separability of the objective function, and yields a high-probability out-of-sample guarantee for the resulting robust problem. We then introduce a penalty-based approximation of this formulation and develop a communication-efficient algorithm called BiDRO-FedAvg, for which we establish a convergence guarantee. We validate the proposed framework through a market-demand prediction simulation.

papers.title: Quadrature-Induced Local Minima in Structure-Preserving Lotka-Volterra Control
papers.abstract: Harvest quadrature can change a discrete optimal control problem even when the state scheme stays fixed. We study this effect for a positivity-preserving Lotka--Volterra scheme. The difference appears in a model with harvesting alone: rewarding the scheme's removal flux gives a strictly convex reduced cost, whereas using prey density at the start of each step overestimates harvest and can create negative curvature and a strict local minimum that is not global. Rational root isolation certifies the two-step global minimizers. With diffusion in one space dimension, nonnegative bounded $H^1$ initial data and positive diffusivities, the costs, weighted gradients and Hessians differ by $O(\tau)$ uniformly in the spatial mesh, where $\tau$ is the time step. A uniform positive lower bound on the reduced Hessian gives the same order for the distance between nearby controls. A large enough effort penalty gives unique global discrete minimizers. We also prove positivity, exact population balance and a common variational limit, and derive exact discrete adjoints and Hessian actions. Numerical tests trace changes in curvature and stationary controls across parameters and grids, with costs evaluated on a common reference using adaptive time stepping. The construction extends to weighted production--destruction systems, giving exact harvest accounting and smooth derivatives on fixed grids.

papers.title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
papers.abstract: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and R\"ossler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

papers.title: Averaged-Cost Control with Shared Feedback under Model Uncertainty
papers.abstract: This paper studies the shared-feedback design problem for finite-horizon averaged-cost control under model uncertainty represented by a joint law over the model parameter and initial state. One feedback map is shared across all realizations and uses only time and the current state as online inputs. We develop two methods: the nonlinear adjoint method combines forward closed-loop solves, backward adjoints, and joint-law policy gradients, while the linear moment method gives exact cost and gradient formulas for a homogeneous linear-quadratic design model by propagating conditional second moments. Numerical studies compare averaged and nominal designs for time-dependent neural feedback and static linear feedback in nonlinear Van der Pol and Stuart-Landau systems; the static gains are designed from oscillator linearizations and evaluated on the original nonlinear systems. Averaged design has lower cost in most comparisons.
